open_obligations: Note that no RL agent is trained, so learning speed with sparse reward is not measured.
Check that synthetic labels from PRMlarge are a fair stand-in for expensive human labels.
Check the reported underperformance at 200 samples per problem before extrapolating the 2.6x figure.
in.other_title: Active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions gives ~2.6x data efficiency
in.rationale: Amodei et al. propose actively requested reward samples as a step for semi-supervised RL. Lightman et al. estimate that active learning on convincing wrong-answer solutions is about 2.6x more data efficient than uniform labelling when training process reward models; the supervision is synthetic (from a large PRM), the learner is a reward model, and no RL agent is trained.
in.scope: proposed SAME_QUESTION_DIFFERENT_SETTING: whether actively choosing which samples get expensive supervision improves data efficiency, for reward samples in Atari RL (an experiment Amodei et al. propose) versus labels for training process reward models (Lightman et al.)

text: The authors propose testing semi-supervised RL in basic control tasks such as cartpole or pendulum swing-up and ask whether, with reward on a random 10% of episodes, an agent can learn nearly as quickly as with reward every episode. Next steps they suggest are Atari with actively requested reward samples, then tasks with complex reward, possibly provided directly by a human if learning is data-efficient enough.
title: Proposed experiments: can RL learn nearly as fast with reward on 10% of episodes?
